title: Love your enemies (Luke 6:27–38)
hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon on the plain began with blessings and woes. Your line was blessed are you poor. Who did you give to? Day four hundred fifty-four.

Picture a market stall in Galilee selling grain. You hold out a measuring basket. A stingy seller scoops loosely, so there's air in it. A generous one fills it, presses it down with his hands, gives it a shake so the grain settles, fills it again until it heaps and spills over the rim. Then he pours it into the fold of your robe, which people used like a big pocket. You walk away with more than you paid for. Jesus ends one of his hardest teachings with that picture. Today, what comes before it.
screen: `A MEASURING BASKET AT A STALL.` → `PRESSED, SHAKEN, SPILLING OVER.` → `POURED INTO YOUR LAP.`

segments.voice: The sermon on the plain keeps going, and it gets harder. "But I say to you that hear: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you." Then, one after another: bless those who curse you. Pray for those who mistreat you. If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other. Give to everyone who asks. Do to others as you'd have them do to you. Notice that love here is not a feeling. Every item is an action: do good, bless, pray, give. Jesus doesn't ask you to like your enemy. He asks you to act for their good. Then he gives the reason: be merciful, as your Father also is merciful. God, he says, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom." For with the same measure that you use, it will be measured back to you. That's not a business deal. It's about the size of your basket. People who measure out mercy with a tiny scoop tend to live in a tiny world. Luke, who wrote this Gospel, also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, and he shows it happening. Stephen, the first martyr, dies under the stones praying for the people throwing them. Catholics honor many saints who did the same. It's the hardest line in the sermon, and the Church has never pretended otherwise. It also never says an enemy stops being dangerous. Loving an enemy can mean keeping a safe distance and still praying for them.
screen: `LOVE HERE IS ACTION, NOT FEELING.` · `BE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER IS.` · `THE SIZE OF YOUR BASKET.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS UNDER THE STONES.` · then, large: `GOOD MEASURE, RUNNING OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one enemy by name. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who has hurt you or works against you. It doesn't have to be the worst one. Start small. Say their name inside, once. Notice what happens in your chest. Then, if you pray, ask God for one good thing for them: health, peace, a better day than they gave you. If you don't pray, simply wish it for them. You don't have to feel warm. You only have to do it. The bell holds the time.
Love your enemies. In Luke, love is something you do: do good, bless, pray, give, with a generous measure. Today's word.
Your line: good measure. Today, when you give anything, time, patience, a tip, an answer, press it down and let it spill over a little. Day four hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for enemies in personal prayer and in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and the Church counts praying for the living, including those who wrong us, among the spiritual works of mercy.

myth: in Luke, loving an enemy means feeling warmly toward them
every command is an action: do good, bless, pray, give.
the running-over measure is poured into the fold of a robe
Luke 6:38 says into your bosom: the fold of a garment used like a pocket.
Luke also wrote Acts, where Stephen prays for those stoning him
Acts 7:60: Stephen asks the Lord not to lay this sin to their charge.

fork.setup: someone who has wronged you asks you for a favor today. by Luke 6, what's the move?
options: do it, and give a little more than they asked.
do it, but make sure they know you're keeping score.
fork.reveal: Luke 6 says give to everyone who asks, and give good measure. the measure you use is the measure you'll get back.

original.note: Greek: love your enemies. The verb is from agape, the love that acts for another's good.

trapdoor: what you thought: love your enemies means pretending you're not hurt.
what it means: it means acting for their good: blessing, praying, giving, with a generous measure, even while you keep yourself safe.
what a scholar hears: Luke ties it to God's character: be merciful (oiktirmones), as your Father is merciful, where Matthew says be perfect.

sources.quoted: But I say to you that hear: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you.
Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 6:27 and 6:38.
The grain-market picture (pressing and shaking a measure) is the standard background reading of Luke 6:38; confirm.
The note that loving an enemy can include keeping a safe distance is pastoral framing for listeners in abusive situations; confirm it fits Catholic teaching.
howItsDone: 'pray for the living and the dead' is the spiritual work of mercy (CCC 2447); confirm phrasing.
